title: Break The Spin · Nov 17
subtitle: 5 posts, all real photos, for Nov 17 (one slot to be a story).

posts.theme: Mamdani disbands the NYPD's riot unit
posts.quote: MAMDANI JUST DISBANDED THE NYPD'S RIOT UNIT. PROTESTS NOW GO TO CIVILIAN TEAMS WITH NO WEAPONS AND NO ARREST POWERS.
posts.alt: Photo of NYPD Strategic Response Group officers standing in a line at a demonstration, with a red-ringed circle inset of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Bold text below reads: Mamdani just disbanded the NYPD's riot unit. Protests now go to civilian teams with no weapons and no arrest powers.
posts.caption:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani just kept one of his biggest campaign promises, and New York's police unions are furious.

The mayor and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, the unit that handles riots and large protests, is being disbanded. Protest response will be led by a new Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division inside the Mayor's Office of Community Safety. In the mayor's office's own words, it "will not have weapons or arrest powers."

A 30-officer First Amendment Support Team will handle dialogue at demonstrations, and the unit's counterterrorism work moves to an existing command. Mamdani says protest response and counterterrorism "are not the same, and they should be separated." Tisch, who had argued for reforming the unit rather than scrapping it, insisted, "I would never compromise on security for New Yorkers."

Police Benevolent Association president Patrick Hendry fired back: "Mayor Mamdani is showing his true colors: He's willing to put our safety and police officers' safety at risk."
posts.first:
Detectives' union president Scott Munro said disbanding the unit "proves just how disconnected City Hall is from the realities of policing in New York City." He pointed to 2024, when clearing an occupied building at Columbia University took a police operation and more than 100 arrests.

Now the lead role at a protest goes to a team that cannot arrest anyone. Munro warned detectives "will now be pulled away from investigating crimes" to fill the gap.

The right to protest is protected. Riots are not. New York just made it harder to tell the difference on the street.

posts.theme: Probation for a gunman who shot a kid
posts.quote: DARIUS DREW, 19, FIRED 20+ SHOTS AND HIT A KID PLAYING BASKETBALL IN D.C. PROSECUTORS WANTED 5 YEARS. AN OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE GAVE HIM PROBATION.
posts.alt: Two panels: a U.S. Attorney's Office photo of two black handguns recovered from the shooter's bedroom on the left and a photo of Judge Jennifer Di Toro on the right. Bold text below reads: Darius Drew, 19, fired 20+ shots and hit a kid playing basketball in D.C. Prosecutors wanted 5 years. An Obama-appointed judge gave him probation.
posts.caption:
Prosecutors say 19-year-old Darius Drew fired more than 20 rounds into a Northwest Washington, D.C., neighborhood in May, shooting from two different spots. One bullet hit a boy who was playing basketball at a recreation center, striking him in the leg. Federal prosecutors say surveillance video caught him firing at a parked car, and a search of his home turned up two guns, ammunition and large amounts of suspected narcotics.

Drew pleaded guilty to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license. Prosecutors asked for five years behind bars. D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro, an Obama appointee, instead suspended a two-year prison sentence and gave him 18 months of supervised probation under the city's Youth Rehabilitation Act. He walked out after nearly six months in custody.

The White House called the case an example of "the insanity of Washington, D.C.'s soft-on-crime policies," which spokeswoman Lauren Bis said give adults "just a slap on the wrist."
posts.first:
The Youth Rehabilitation Act lets D.C. judges sentence offenders under 25 below the mandatory minimums. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro has been pressing Congress to change it. Writing about another case in 2025, she said that sentence "was a legal sentence only because he was sentenced under the YRA."

Prosecutors had opposed both his release and the use of the YRA.

A child was shot while playing basketball, and the man who fired the gun was home before Thanksgiving.

Second chances matter for young people who make mistakes. Firing 20 rounds into a neighborhood is not a mistake. A law that treats it like one is a message to the next shooter.

posts.theme: Seattle strips Andrew Jackson's name from a park
posts.quote: SEATTLE'S SOCIALIST MAYOR IS STRIPPING ANDREW JACKSON'S NAME OFF A PARK THAT HAS CARRIED IT SINCE 1928. THE SEVENTH PRESIDENT IS THE LEFT'S LATEST TARGET.
posts.alt: Two panels: a painted portrait of President Andrew Jackson on the left and a photo of Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson on the right. Bold text below reads: Seattle's socialist mayor is stripping Andrew Jackson's name off a park that has carried it since 1928. The seventh president is the left's latest target.
posts.caption:
Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson has ordered the city's parks department to take Andrew Jackson's name off Jackson Park, the 160-acre park and public golf course in north Seattle that has been named for him since 1928.

"I'm directing Seattle Parks and Recreation to begin a community naming process," Wilson said, adding, "Now is the right time to move this conversation forward." The city points to Jackson's role in the forced removal of Native Americans. Public suggestions for a new name are due December 14. A naming committee will recommend a replacement, and the parks superintendent gets the final say. Interim superintendent Michele Finnegan said community input will help make Jackson Park "a place where everyone feels safe."

Andrew Jackson was the seventh president, the general who beat the British at New Orleans in the War of 1812, and the founder of the modern Democratic Party. For nearly a century, Seattle saw no problem with that.
posts.first:
Jackson's record includes the Indian Removal Act and slavery, and Americans should learn all of it, the good and the bad. Taking his name off a golf course teaches none of it. It just removes him from view. And apparently a golf course was not safe enough with a president's name on it.

Democrats used to hold Jefferson-Jackson dinners every year to honor the founders of their party. Now one of those founders is too offensive for a city park.

Every renaming fight gets sold as the last one. It never is. Today it is a park named for a president from the 1830s. The list only gets longer from here.

posts.theme: U.S. Attorney warns Warren to preserve her records
posts.quote: A FEDERAL PROSECUTOR JUST WARNED ELIZABETH WARREN: DON'T DESTROY ANY RECORDS ABOUT YOUR PLANNED PROBES OF TRUMP ALLIES, OR FACE LEGAL CONSEQUENCES.
posts.alt: Two panels: official portrait photos of Sen. Elizabeth Warren on the left and U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz on the right. Bold text below reads: A federal prosecutor just warned Elizabeth Warren: don't destroy any records about your planned probes of Trump allies, or face legal consequences.
posts.caption:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren has been promising payback since Democrats won the Senate. She is the top Democrat on the Banking Committee, is set to chair it in January, and has warned that people "better get ready for some investigations, serious ones."

Now a federal prosecutor has answered her. Aaron Reitz, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas and a former chief of staff to Sen. Ted Cruz, sent Warren a letter giving her "formal notice of your obligation to preserve all documents" tied to her plans. He accused her of planning "to target private individuals close to President Trump." Failing to comply, he wrote, "may carry significant legal consequences." She has until November 23 to confirm in writing that she has done it.

Reitz did not hold back. "You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk," he wrote, calling the letter his "first arrow shot." Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Elissa Slotkin received letters too.
posts.first:
To be fair, the letter does not accuse Warren of breaking any law, and the Constitution gives Congress broad protection for legitimate investigations.

But Democrats know this playbook well. Warren herself has sent preservation demands to Trump officials, including one to Attorney General Pam Bondi in January. Now the same standard is being applied to her. Whether the letter holds up legally or not, the message landed.

If senators plan to use their gavels to go after private citizens for being "close" to the president, they should expect to be held to the same rules they want to enforce on everyone else.

posts.theme: NJ governor vs. Rutgers Republicans over Bovino
posts.quote: NEW JERSEY'S DEMOCRAT GOVERNOR SLAMMED COLLEGE REPUBLICANS FOR INVITING TRUMP'S BORDER CHIEF TO SPEAK AT RUTGERS. THE STUDENTS: FREE SPEECH IS A "GOD GIVEN RIGHT."
posts.alt: Two panels: official portrait photo of New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill on the left and a photo of former Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino in uniform on the right. Bold text below reads: New Jersey's Democrat governor slammed college Republicans for inviting Trump's border chief to speak at Rutgers. The students: free speech is a "god given right."
posts.caption:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill publicly scolded the Rutgers College Republicans for inviting former Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino to speak on campus.

"I'm deeply disappointed in the Rutgers Republicans Club's decision to invite Greg Bovino to speak on campus," Sherrill posted. "Giving him a platform is the wrong decision." She urged attendees to ask him "why he chose cruelty over humanity."

The students did not back down. "It is deeply troubling that the governor of a free nation is condemning" what they called "a basic, universal, and god given right to free speech," the club wrote. "Condemning us for our universal basic right sets an extremely dangerous precedent."

Bovino answered her himself: "Spoken like a true lib who puts illegals aliens before her own citizens." Opponents launched a petition to keep him off campus and planned a counterprotest.
posts.first:
Even Rutgers sided with the students on the basics, saying the club is a recognized student group allowed to host speakers and the university is "committed to protecting free expression."

Club president Andrew Joseph put it simply: "We believe in the open market of ideas." The club first tried to book Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback before landing Bovino, who has reportedly explored a 2028 presidential bid.

That used to be the whole point of a university. A governor does not have to like a speaker. But when the state's top official tells students who they should not invite, every conservative student in New Jersey hears the message. Free speech that only covers speakers the governor approves of is not free speech.
